title: Privacy-Preserving Intelligence — Steve Korshakov, Bee (acq. Amazon)
talk_summary: Steve Korshakov describes Bee's privacy-preserving architecture for an always-on personal AI wearable: keys held only on the user's phone, remote attestation against a transparency log, confidential-compute inference nodes, and 7-day forced key expiration. The talk is mostly about end-to-end encryption and supply-chain attestation for a consumer device, not about agent orchestration efficiency.

takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than trying to prompt or train agents to behave, they constrain what an agent can physically do by running it in a sandbox with no path to cause harm.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I think nothing works except like sandboxing and just not giving them a way to hurt themselves.

takeaways.what_they_do: Any key material held in memory on a node has a hard 7-day expiration, chosen as the realistic horizon for useful work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we introduced everywhere where we have the keys in the memory uh uh the forced expiration of seven days.

takeaways.what_they_do: A separate team controls signing keys hardcoded into clients; the shipping team cannot push changes unnoticed, and base images are signed separately from deploy manifests to keep the slow approval path off the hot path.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we split it in two parts so like the first one is to build the base image

takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately kept custom code to ~20k lines in a memory-safe language, reusing trusted off-the-shelf software instead of building their own, so the security-critical surface stays auditable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's just like about 20k lines on memory safe language. So it was very small scope that we were able to audit
